subsubtopic: EDUCATIONAL PROGRAMMING-NEGOTIATIONS WITH PROVINCES ON LICENSING OF STATIONS-DETERMINATION OF CONTENT-REVOKING OF LICENCES OF PROVINCIAL AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State who has made statements to the press that he has a mandate from the cabinet to pursue negotiations with the provinces on the subject of licensing broadcasting stations to broadcast educational material. In view of the confusion and vaccilation in the last couple of years on this whole subject, can the minister indicate briefly to the House the specific scope of his mandate from the government in this area?
.

subsubtopic: EDUCATIONAL PROGRAMMING-NEGOTIATIONS WITH PROVINCES ON LICENSING OF STATIONS-DETERMINATION OF CONTENT-REVOKING OF LICENCES OF PROVINCIAL AGENCIES
speechtext:
I think, Mr. Speaker, that I can resume it rather briefly.

December 9, 1971
Inquiries of the Ministry
Some Canadian provinces, especially Alberta, Ontario and Quebec approached us many months ago. The cabinet has studied the matter and has asked me to meet the provincial ministers concerned in order to consider the possibility of making a new arrangement. The cabinet has also stated three conditions which would be set by the federal government, providing an agreement acceptable to the provinces and ourselves would finally be reached.
The first condition is that the authority of the CRTC and the jurisdiction of the federal government in the broadcasting field remain complete. In the second place, the stations which would air educational programs in the provinces would have to comply with the definition of educational broadcasting drawn up, in agreement with the ten provinces, two years ago. The third is that the licences would not be delivered by a provincial government or one of its departments, but as it is done at the federal level, by a body independent of the provincial executive.

subsubtopic: EDUCATIONAL PROGRAMMING-NEGOTIATIONS WITH PROVINCES ON LICENSING OF STATIONS-DETERMINATION OF CONTENT-REVOKING OF LICENCES OF PROVINCIAL AGENCIES
speechtext: In these negotiations is it contemplated that one of the conditions shall be that the CRTC will be the judge of what is considered to be educational content that might be broadcast by one of these stations licensed under this proposal?

subsubtopic: EDUCATIONAL PROGRAMMING-NEGOTIATIONS WITH PROVINCES ON LICENSING OF STATIONS-DETERMINATION OF CONTENT-REVOKING OF LICENCES OF PROVINCIAL AGENCIES
speechtext: That is to say, Mr. Speaker, that the CRTC would have no judgment to pass on the quality since the definition of educational television has already been accepted by the provinces. The CRTC would only pass judgment on facts, that is to say, it would merely say whether such and such an educational program is, I say it again, generally different from ordinary broadcasts.

subsubtopic: EDUCATIONAL PROGRAMMING-NEGOTIATIONS WITH PROVINCES ON LICENSING OF STATIONS-DETERMINATION OF CONTENT-REVOKING OF LICENCES OF PROVINCIAL AGENCIES
speechtext: Since these negotiations contemplate the rescinding of the directive issued by the government in June, 1970, I think, which directed that there should be no renewal of these licences to stations which were in fact provincial agencies for educational purposes, is the government prepared to revoke that directive now so that these stations will not have this axe hanging over their heads and bargaining can proceed in good faith?

subsubtopic: EDUCATIONAL PROGRAMMING-NEGOTIATIONS WITH PROVINCES ON LICENSING OF STATIONS-DETERMINATION OF CONTENT-REVOKING OF LICENCES OF PROVINCIAL AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are seeking a solution so that the stations that the Leader of the Opposition is referring to may continue to transmit radio programs; this is indeed in the field of radio only. I do not believe however that it should be through educational TV that we may solve the problem of these radio stations. One of the complications is that they are not really transmitting educational radio programs, but general broadcasting of a cultural nature.
But efforts to find a solution allowing these stations, connected with universities, to keep on broadcasting have not ceased. The CRTC and we ourselves are still trying to find it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
This House calls on the government to institute without delay policies and programs designed to arrest further expansion of foreign control of Canada's economy and to regain control by the Canadian people of our natural resources and manufacturing and service industries in order to assure our country's independence and jobs for Canadian workers and to enable Canadians to shape their own national identity and social values.
December 9, 1971

He said: Mr. Speaker, I placed the motion which you have just read on the order paper for two reasons. The first one relates to the fatuous statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) after his return from Washington last Monday. It seemed clear to us that he came back from Washington with empty hands.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Not at all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
In a desperate search to justify the trip which he may have made reluctantly, he tried to inflate a simple and natural remark by the President of the United States into nothing less than a breakthrough for Canada. Mr. Nixon was kind enough to say that he recognized Canada's right to be independent in all spheres. What else one would have expected him to say I do not know. That, as I gathered from the Prime Minister, should be sufficient to remove all our worries and to guarantee our independence for all time. We can all relax now. The President of the United States assured our Prime Minister that he does not intend to treat Canada like a colony. We need have no more worries. President Nixon spoke. The Prime Minister heard it. No doubt they shook hands on it and that is, to use the Prime Minister's adjective, fantastic. I say, what fatuous nonsense.
The second reason for placing the present motion before the House is the failure of the government to announce its policy on foreign investment and the numerous indications showing that when it does announce it, the policy will be without teeth and without the capacity for regaining control of Canada's economy over the years ahead. For years concerned Canadians have been waiting for government policy and action to check and reverse the increasing foreign control of our economy. Since Walter Gordon's days in 1963, Liberal governments have been fumbling helplessly for such a policy. They have been fumbling because they have not been serious about the subject. Their traditional continentalism, their anxiety not to interfere with the power of their corporate friends and their doctrinaire reliance on outmoded private enterprise shibboleths have rendered them incapable of protecting Canada's independence. That is why they have thrashed about without result.
For some two years, Mr. Speaker, the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) has been charged with the job of developing recommendations on policy. The other day the Prime Minister suggested that the government has finally reached four firm decisions but that he would not announce them until he was able to publish some of the studies on which these decisions are based. It is impossible for me, Sir, to understand the delay in announcing the policy.
Let us look at the history of this matter, Mr. Speaker. At first it was suggested that the studies were papers for the eyes of the cabinet only. Then, one of those papers, a preliminary one apparently, found its way to the Canadian Forum. This was followed by the leak of a cabinet document containing a decision on principle. Following that, we were told that the government would be prepared to consider what studies to publish, if any. Now, the publication of these studies has become so important and crucial that the announcement of a policy is to be delayed until that publication takes place. I cannot help saying
Control of Canadian Economy
that strange and tortuous indeed are the workings of the collective mind of this government.
I want to make clear on behalf of our party that we are desperately concerned about the future of our country and the continuing erosion of our effective independence by the massive foreign control of our economy, and about the distortions which that control has created in our industrial development. We are concerned about this not for any reason of arid nationalism but for very concrete reasons affecting Canadian jobs and the shape not only of our economic destiny but of our national identity and culture as well. Having travelled across Canada, it is my observation that a new Canadian awakening is taking shape. Canadians are increasingly realizing that every aspect of their lives, economic, cultural and even recreational, is invaded by foreign domination. Increasingly, they find it difficult to see how we can build a real sense of Canadian identity so long as we remain a minor dependency of our powerful and overwhelming neighbour.
I also want to make it clear that no sensible person in Canada can fail to realize that we must maintain close and friendly relations with the United States. Geography, history and language make that unavoidable as well as desirable. I maintain, and our party maintains, that a friendship founded in equality is honourable and productive. However, a relationship based on the timidity of a satellite is humiliating and sterile.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
The New Democratic Party wants to see a policy of continuing friendship with the people of the United States and with the government of that country, as with the governments of all countries, but not at the expense of our losing the capacity effectively to shape our own economic and social destiny and our own social values in a distinct society. The fact is the huge size of foreign equity in the Canadian economy and the large areas of control by multinational corporations present modern Canadian nationalism with immense problems.
I want to make clear at the very start that we appreciate the existence of these problems. We know that the changes we are seeking cannot be achieved overnight. We know it will require years to rid Canada of its dangerous economic dependency. It is precisely for this reason that we condemn the failure of Liberal and Conservative governments over the years to even make a start. The fact is that our governments have not only failed to make a start, they have allowed the foreign controlled sector of the economy to increase every year. They have not only permitted accelerating take-over and expansion of foreign take-over and control, but they continue to invite it. The problem has grown in size every year and the government of Canada carries the major responsibility for the resulting difficulties.
Before I go any further, I want to put on record that our party believes that a policy of foreign ownership must be implemented without delay. I also want to put on record that for such a policy to be effective, it must at least contain the following elements if we are to tackle the problem with imagination and determination.
First, we urge that a screening or control agency be established without delay which will at least have the

December 9, 1971
Control of Canadian Economy
powers suggested in the study published in the Canadian Forum, namely the power to obtain all relevant information to investigate particular industries or practices, to limit take-overs and the further expansion of foreign ownership and control. Unless the agency has these powers, particularly the power to limit further foreign expansion in Canada, it will be a toothless and useless exercise.
Second, we urge that we require a revamped Canada Development Corporation totally different from the distortion that the government produced. The Canadian economy in general, and the provinces in particular, must have an alternative source of investment capital. That can be provided most effectively by a Canada Development Corporation directly under the control and management of the government and responsible through a minister to Parliament. To be really effective, the corporation will require massive investment funds which in our view can be drawn only from the reserves of financial and other corporations as well as other voluntary investment by individual Canadians.
Third, we urge that the Canada Development Corporation must have the authority and the duty to act as an instrument of government planning and development policy and to invest in new industrial development as well as to buy into existing multinational corporations.
Fourth, it must also have the power to invest heavily in research and development, either directly or in partnership with private corporations, in order to encourage new initiatives in this field and develop a Canadian technology so that our dependence on multinational corporations for technological known-how is reduced and eventually limited.
Fifth, the Canada Development Corporation should have the authority and duty to expand the public sector of the economy, either through Crown corporations or through consortium arrangements with private concerns.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
This, I suggest, is obviously the most reliable road to Canadian economic independence. It will not only enable us to develop new sectors of the economy under Canadian control, but also to introduce Canadian ownership and control in resource and manufacturing industries now largely under foreign control. Merely to indicate the powers that we believe the Canada Development Corporation should have is to underline the ineffectiveness and the inadequacy of the kind of corporation that is now on the statute books, one which worries, as it does, about getting into its hands existing Crown corporations rather than worrying about buying into multinational corporations now controlling Canada's economy.
Six, we must introduce a new industrial strategy containing a program of rationalization and specialization in the Canadian manufacturing industry, designed both to meet more of our domestic demand, and thus rely less on imports, and to change our trade pattern away from one predominant market, the market of the United States.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Seven, we urge something that was proposed three years ago in the Watkins report. We urge the immediate establishment of a government export trade
agency with real power to ensure that all corporations in Canada promote trade in accordance with Canadian laws and policies and do not, as subsidiary corporations have in the past, submit to foreign laws and foreign policies.
Eight, in co-operation with the provinces, we must establish standards of resource planning and development and require a great deal more processing of raw materials in Canada instead of shipping not only the materials but also jobs out of this country.
Nine, it is essential to increase public investment in our resource industries, either through public ownership or joint participation with private corporations and, indeed, through both. This is the most, if not the only, effective way of regaining control of our energy and mineral resources which are now mainly in the hands of multinational corporations and world cartels. The government tax bill which is before us continues the tax concessions to the multinational corporations to encourage them still further to gobble up our natural resources, particularly in the field of energy resources.
Ten, and finally, we must implement a policy regarding plant shutdowns in this country, a policy that will require full disclosure of facts before the shutdown is authorized and will enable the government to take-over plants threatened with a shutdown if the operation is economically sound and socially useful for society and the workers in Canada.
I have summarized some of our proposals because we all expect a statement of policy by the government in the near future. I wanted to indicate now the concrete steps which our party believes are essential if we are serious about developing Canadian independence and ensuring the future prosperity of our people. I urge that we rid our minds of what I believe to be a number of myths. It is usually suggested that we need foreign investment because we haven't enough in Canada. This is clearly wrong as has been shown statistically many times. For the last number of years there has not been a shortage of investment capital in this country. The failure has been in the lack of planning and direction. In any case, foreign ownership costs Canada well over a billion dollars annually in interest, dividends, management and licence fees, development and other charges, so that net benefit is, on occasion, a negative quantity.
Canadian businessmen have also developed tne habit of a strange kind of self-denigration by suggesting that they do not have the spirit of entrepreneural adventure. I do not believe this. Their willingness to invite multinational corporations is not due to any lack of capacity; it is due primarily to a desire to make a fast buck by chumming up with the powerful at the expense of Canada's destiny. Through the years Canada has produced tycoons of considerable strength. I may not agree with them but I admire their achievements. We could have more of them. In any case, I reject the notion that a people which has built Canada from wilderness and rock is incapable of generating the capacities to build its own economic future. We have lacked only the will, not the resources, whether financial, material or human.
Our failure is also due, in my opinion, to our exclusive reliance on private corporations to develop our economy.

December 9, 1971

We have permitted wealth to be concentrated in a few hands, most of them foreign hands, and our social and economic structure to remain unchanged. Our values continue to be shaped by the selfish goals of the powerful, rather than by the sensitivity and needs of our people. We shall not overcome our problem if we continue to rely on private corporate goals motivated primarily to maximize profits and power. We can take charge of our economic destiny only if we are prepared to challenge private corporate power, to increase the power of ordinary Canadians to plan their society collectively, with a new industrial structure designed to satisfy the needs of Canadians, and, indeed, the needs of people throughout the world.
Present American policies have underlined the dangers in our present position. Our party has warned about them for years, but they have now become real in the life of Canada and its people. The American surtax and, even more, other protectionist policies like the tax incentives and DISC programs will affect not only our trade but the jobs of Canadians. American multinational corporations may well find it more profitable to take advantage of the immense tax exemptions promised in the United States and transfer the operation of subsidiaries to that country, thus shutting down or reducing operations in Canada with the loss not only of jobs but of essential economic activity.
The government study published by the Canadian Forum emphasizes that foreign ownership and control of our economy means that our social and economic purposes are set by multinational enterprises in boardrooms outside Canada rather than by Canadians. It is natural that people should be concerned about any fundamental changes in the economic pattern and in the industrial strategy of the country. I accept it as natural that they should fear the possibility of dislocation and possible loss of jobs. I want to say to the people of Canada that we see no reason for these fears if, and only if, the essential changes in the control of our economy are carefully planned and if governments, both federal and provincial, take the responsibility which is theirs to assure job security for the Canadian people. This is a responsibility which the federal government has abandoned and betrayed during the past two years by deliberately slowing down the economy and creating massive unemployment crisis-

speechtext:
-from which we shall not be able to emerge for two years at least.
I notice that today the Ontario government released the report of a task force composed of civil servants on the question of foreign ownership. I also note from a press report that the Premier of the province refuses to state a policy until the federal government has done so. This is another example of the lack of seriousness with which governments of this country have treated and are treating the basic problem of Canada's economic independence. The provincial government waits for the federal government. The federal government points to provincial anxieties as a reason for its inaction or inadequate action. In the meantime, the loss of our economic sovereignty continues unchecked and the threat to Canadian political, social and international independence becomes daily more dangerous.
Control of Canadian Economy
My colleagues and I believe passionately that the overriding goal of a modern democratic society must be to eliminate every form of exploitation, to eliminate as far as possible inequalities between regions, and inequalities between groups within each region.

Perhaps the hon. member would have the patience to wait until I have finished, when I shall be glad to listen to a question which I am sure will be relevant as well as earth-shaking.
Our objective must surely be an egalitarian society in which every individual has an equal opportunity to share in a rich and varied life and to develop his talents to the full. Only in such a society, a society in which human equality is the overriding consideration, can the worth and dignity of the human being receive full recognition and respect. I say that a society in which one out of every four or five lives in poverty, a society in which hundreds of thousands are forced into idleness, a society in which the difference in income and living standards between regions and among groups, remains intolerable, is an unjust society and that speeches about the worth and dignity of the individual in these circumstances sound just as hollow as in fact they are.
I say to you, Sir, that we cannot talk seriously about a just society as long as we continue to rely primarily on the benevolence of corporations whose purpose is not first and foremost the common good and whose activities are frequently in conflict with the aspirations and needs of ordinary people. We must drop our old-fashioned, doctrinaire ideas about our society and recognize the need for increasing public participation, the need for increasing collective effort to achieve desirable national goals.

These are the reasons a democratic socialist party like ours believes that the question of foreign ownership and control is crucial to the people of Canada. I suggest to you that Canada is already fighting for its very life. Any further delay is to betray our people.
I put it this strongly because of my profound faith in our country. Canada, perhaps more than any other country, has the resources, financial, physical and human, to satisfy the anxious search of mankind for new social structures from which poverty and want, inequality and waste, may eventually be eliminated. I have a deep faith in the capacity of our ordinary people, in their political strength and in their belief in their country. All they need is courageous and imaginative leadership. Certainly, the heavy emphasis in my friend's resolution and in his speech was on the question of ownership. I do not deny that the question of ownership can be relevant and, in certain sectors, very important. We have maintained this in the past and we maintain it today. There are obvious sectors, such as finance, insurance and communications, and there may well be others, where it is important to keep a close watch and where we should be prepared to move. I do not rule out a screening process, for example, for new investment of the kind that would bring about some distortion in our economic priorities in this country. We should be willing to consider these possibilities. But first of all let us be clear as to what our priorities are. Quite apart from that, what we should not be doing and what we must not do, under the guise of creating some sort of screen to preserve our nationhood and on the pretext of saving Canadian independence, is to create new bureaucratic monstrosities with arbitrary powers over the economy which would destroy, not simply economic freedom but economic growth and development in this country.
Let us not forget that there are other aspects of the independence and autonomy of our country which are at least as relevant to us as is the ownership of property. There is trade. In a country that achieves 25 per cent of its gross national product through external trade-over 80 per cent of our manufactured goods go to one country, the United States-surely the concentration of trade in this way is just as important in relation to the autonomy and independence of our country as is any concentration of ownership. The official policy of the government has been multilateralism, but in fact what has developed has been a continental trading pattern. That has been the real Liber-

al policy. In view of the degree of interdependence that has developed between Canada and the United States we need guidelines to govern our behaviour. I am not minimizing the importance of trying to diversify our trade with the European Economic Community, for example, but one must be realistic and recognize the importance of the U.S. market at this stage in time. Therefore, if we are going to maintain a position of comfort in our economy, we must recognize the importance of establishing meaningful guidelines which would govern the behaviour of Washington and Ottawa toward each other. The sad truth is that the government is lacking in any strategy of economic development. I could develop this aspect at some length but my time is very limited. We have had piecemeal efforts at tax reform, at curing economic disparity, at a competition act, and now, from what we hear, the government has made up its mind about a foreign investment policy, all without any regard to any over-all strategy of economic development. We have had it with regard to taxation; now, apparently we will have it with regard to foreign ownership. I am sure that since the government has made up its mind, anything I say here today will have very little effect. However, there are some things I want to say in any event.
I expect that the government will go off half-cocked once again, not for lack of time but because of its failure to develop any general economic strategy, the need for which was emphasized even by those who wrote what was described as the leaked Gray report. They recognized that to have an effective or meaningful screening process with regard to foreign development there had to be a government strategy of development which this screening process was supposed to implement. But what the authors of that report overlooked was that the very machinery that might be established can only be significant, intelligible and intelligent if it is related to some decisions on priorities and decisions that have been taken with regard to an industrial strategy which we do not have at all. Nobody

need take my word for this. The Science Council of Canada has made it very clear that this government has no industrial strategy.
I recognize that in certain areas in particular, foreign ownership may be a problem. That is not the most basic problem with which we are faced. The most basic problem is the lack of any sort of strategy for economic development. This government has failed in many fields, but certainly in this. What we need is a strategy, not only because it will enable us to develop our priorities in terms of industry but because we need something that will enable us to use industry in the broadest sense of the term, including services, farming and natural resources. It is only by setting such priorities that we shall be able to look intelligently at the matter of foreign investment and see what degree of distortion is in fact taking place in relation to the kind of strategy we want to achieve. We should see what steps should be taken in respect of foreign investment to fit it into our own priorities in Canada. A strategy of economic development worked out on high by the federal government, the supergroup or whoever tries to do it, will not mean a thing unless it carries with it the support of the provinces. giving encouragement. It has failed to produce any strategy. We in our party have adopted a positive approach designed to restore confidence and build up the country.
Let us examine the role of foreign investment in the context of a meaningful strategy of economic development to develop our country and to develop its independence. Speaking for myself and for my colleagues, we shall not allow ourselves to be hypnotized by a slogan or by simplistic answers. We need an industrial strategy and we shall in all probability continue to need foreign investment. Our challenge is to reconcile these two goals. Mr. Speaker, we in the opposition are very happy with the motion moved by the New Democratic Party because it gives us the opportunity of restating our confidence in Canada's potentialities and in our international policy, especially with regard to the United States.
Mr. Speaker, while the diplomatic war deliberately carried out by this government with our neighbours to the south goes on in order to justify other diplomatic manoeuvres with the communist world, American control of Canadian resources continues to grow. In this connection, this week the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), following a meeting of barely two hours with President Nixon, stated that both countries had agreed that each one was free to choose its political and economic destinies, while respecting the other.
In short, the right hon. Prime Minister went and asked Mr. Nixon if Canada was a country separate from the United States. Mr. Nixon replied: Yes, of course. That does not mean anything. Those are the terms with which the Prime Minister is content. But facts are the extreme opposite of the political strategy of the Liberal party that keeps on handing out Canada to Americans for a dish of lentils. But we know it is the federal government that has jurisdiction over foreign investments.
Our relationships are characterized by the interdependence of our two countries in culture, technology, finance, trade and tourism in one word in everything.
December 9, 1971

The present legitimate concerns of the Canadian people which is more than ever determined to attain its independence in North America are deeply rooted in history and in the struggle waged by Canada to carve its own future in spite of the large difference between the size and the power of the two countries.
Mr. Speaker, the concerns of Canadians, which are shared by the Social Credit Party of Canada, are linked first of all to recent social and economic events which are today more acute and alarming. My time being limited, I shall only mention them. They are: the profound influence of American culture on Canada's and Quebec's way of life, the extent to which our industries and resources are controlled by Americans, the attraction that the United States offer for Canadian scientists, engineers and professionals who are unable to exercise their talents in their country, the numerical superiority of American teachers in Canadian universities and the predominantly American content of radio and television programs.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, Canadians and Americans should consider these phenomena in the light of their respective history and national aspirations. It was obviously not necessary for the right hon. Prime Minister to go to Washington to acquaint himself of the fact that we are two distinct nations. We must therefore not only take into account the factors which tend to unite our two countries, but also and increasingly so, those past and present factors which tend to separate and divide them.
In fact, it is urgent for Canada to find and attain its own national identity, not only by words of mouth, but in fact.
For the most part, these problems result from the disparity of our respective powers in practically all areas.
In most of their transactions the United States are in a better position to promote or to jeopardize Canadian interests than Canada is to influence American prosperity and security. Canadians are more aware of this situation than the Americans. The recent 10 per cent American surtax on imports is a fair example of those conflicting interests.
Faced with this situation, which is not new, the previous governments, in the pay of almighty finance, have constantly kowtowed and each time we could have orderly and logically imposed ourselves as Canadians and with legitimate national proudness, we hurried to exchanged our natural resources against a handful of peanuts.
What did we do with our iron? We gave it away. We begged the Americans to carry it home so they would employ their own labour, process our products and subsequently sell them back here.

What did we do with our oil?
What did we do with our marine resources?
We are giving them away and, as certain NDP members do, we blame the Americans for it.
We in this party say that the blame rests on former governments which, in the pay of high finance, went running on all fours before these people and begged them to develop our country so as to get votes and then put the blame on the Americans.
We in the Social Credit Party, want to be more honest than that.
So as to prove what I am saying, I shall quote an article from the October 24, 1971 edition of the newspaper Dimanche-Matin, entitled "Mr. Masse is asking the USA oil industry to develop our resources".
That happened in New Orleans. And he is not better than the others. He is not different from them, simply more of the same.
The article was as follows:
Proximity of the markets, co-operation from the Quebec government and recent oil discoveries in Nova Scotia were factors that obviously interested officials of the southern United States oil industry when Quebec Natural Resources Minister Gilles Masse invited them to come and explore for oil fields and develop our oil resources.
Leading a delegation that spent last week in Louisiana, Mr. Masse, accompanied-
After a detailed account we are told that Mr. Masse would extend numerous privileges to the Americans so as to enable them to discover oil in this country, as if Canadians were unable to discover their own natural resources. They go to the United States and say: With the promise of generous tax privileges, and other things, we invite you to come and discover our resources, to take them and develop them; meanwhile, we work in those mines, we develop our resources and nothing is left to us. We are even not wise enough to demand royalties for those natural resources, royalties that would be payable to the government of this country or of the province and that would make it possible to redistribute to the people who own them at least a part of those natural resources. Then, they will blame the Americans.
But in fact, the Americans are filling a vacuum that Canadians refuse to fill because they say they are unable to do it or because their hands are tied. Either Canadians do not possess enough competence to develop their country or they do not have the resources necessary to do it. We think the reason is not that the Canadians are unable to do it but rather that their governments are tied down by the world of finance and prefer to sell out Canada on a long term basis on the pretext of bringing in foreign capital and thus creating jobs.
The governments live from day to day and that is their most serious problem and most serious fault. An attempt has been made to collect detailed financial data on 570 of the 606 separate companies, the excluded companies being mostly financial corporations. These 570 companies had 46 per cent of the assets of all fully tabulated companies in 1964, 35 per cent of the sales, 53 per cent of the taxable income, paid 67 per cent of the dividends and accounted for 51 per cent of the net internal cash flow.
These large companies are a very dominant factor in three sectors of the Canadian economy-mining, quarrying and oil wells,-
These are three sectors where our governments, federal and provincial, instead of availing themselves of the necessary mechanisms to develop our resources for the benefit of the Canadian people, went to the United States and begged our neighbours to come and have them developed on our behalf.
Mr. Speaker, one can recall also that a cabinet minister, the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans), once said publicly that the American influence in those three sectors was too great. He wanted to protest and, then, the Liberal party threw him out. Whom is the Liberal government serving?

Prevoyance which was in the process of being taken over

by Americans. On this side of the House somebody asked the government what it intended to do. The answer was that the problem was of a technical and legal nature and that intervention was impossible.

We asked the government what it proposed to do, but we got no answer. I phoned the office of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, but no answer there either.
This is the situation, Mr. Speaker. And yet, when a liberal or conservative government is brought to power, the first thing it does is to take a yearly trip to Washington or to Wall Street in New York. What for? To obtain funds in order to support provinces, municipalities, school boards and the whole public sector.
We suggest that the Bank of Canada become the main source of funds for the public sector, for provinces, for municipalities, for school boards so that there may be a great flow of Canadian capital, which in turn will be invested in the private sector in order to stimulate our economy.
The reason we have to obtain American capital in order to develop the public sector, which is the most costly-as can be seen when we read the annual reports and balance sheets of municipalities and school boards-is that there is a lack of Canadian capital. Most municipalities in Quebec spend 40 per cent of their budget on public debt payments. As for the federal government, 14 cents out of each tax dollars goes towards paying the interest on the public debt. Therefore the lack of capital in Canada is not surprising since most of the capital available here for developing our country and our natural resources is used to service the public debt.
That is why we are trapped in a vise, stuck in a vicious circle where Canadian capital gets lost and becomes nonproductive; the best we can do is repay the money borrowed in foreign countries where we simply could have asked the Bank of Canada to invest money.
Mr. Speaker, there is more to it than blaming the Americans for lending us money.
If Americans have faith in our natural resources, if they believe in Canada to the extent of heavily investing in it, why should Canadians not also have faith in their country and avail themselves of financial mechanisms to ensure its development through the Bank of Canada? Why should Canadians not have faith in their country, if Americans do?
Mr. Speaker, that is the language Canada's Social Credit uses. We shall not solve our problems by putting the blame on Americans, but by giving Canadians the opportunity to develop their country, by inculcating them with national pride, by making them realize that Canada belongs to them, as do the country's natural resources and that it is up to them, not to foreigners or neighbours, to develop their country.

allowances or some other allowances, to the benefit of the people. Thus the provincial governments were able to reduce personal taxes while increasing the purchasing power of the people.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are in a position to give themselves the financial permission to develop their country- however paradoxical this may seem for some hon. members opposite-though the Bank of Canada.
In conclusion, I wonder how is it that the successive governments for over 30 years have dealt with everything, have made inquiries on everything, have discussed everything in order to solve their problems but have never thought of going to the Bank of Canada.
Reforms have been undertaken in all fields and at all times to find solutions which have been but poultices on wooden legs. What difference is there, Mr. Speaker, between $10, $100 or $1,000 coming from either Washington or New York, and the same amounts coming from the Bank of Canada? The Social Credit Party of Canada is not anti-American. We advocate a policy of good understanding, of exchanges at all levels, of constant co-operation but not at the expense of Canadians.

I want to make a few points that will have a direct bearing and some relationship to the issue before this House. What we heard, perhaps politely put, was "Bob, the Tory" revealing himself. First, we heard the disparaging comments about the suggestion that some public enterprise in this country might indeed be beneficial. He referred to his concern about the Atlantic and other provinces which might be deprived of the advantages accruing from foreign investment. I remind the Leader of the Opposition that, after nearly a century of almost exclusive emphasis on private enterprise, the Atlantic provinces are not exactly one of the richest regions in Canada. The steel industry in his province was notoriously known throughout the steel industry, both in this country and abroad, for losing money annually. After it was brought within public ownership, it made a profit for the first time in many years and is still making a profit. I further remind the Leader of the Opposition that the New Democratic Party never argued we should cut off all sources of investment capital. We have argued that when it comes in, it should be on a minority shareholder basis. Above and beyond that, we have argued for a meaningful Canada Development Corporation that would provide investment capital, not only in the Atlantic provinces and other poor regions, but in many places in this country.
Finally, there was the unjust and inaccurate description of our party's position, and that of the leader of our party, which he stated this afternoon with regard to public ownership. The Leader of the Opposition raised the old shibboleth of 19th century socialism. He said we know what that has led to in certain parts of the world. He said that it has not been very efficient and has not achieved all the wonders its believers thought it would. That is a distortion of what we are arguing for at this time in this Parliament and throughout the country. We have never argued at the provincial and federal levels of this party for anything other than a mixed economy at this time. It is to create a caricature to suggest that all we want is public ownership

December 9, 1971
Control of Canadian Economy
and cite a lot of misleading examples to show that it has run into certain difficulties here and in other parts of the world. We are now talking about a mixed economy. We have ideas. In terms of emphasis in this debate and at other times, we stress that we need more public involvement, not less. We do not want the total absence of all private enterprise in the economy.
I would like to take up the challenge of what should be done with one of the major sectors of the economy in terms of private enterprise at this time. I refer to the automotive industry. The automotive industry in Canada is one of the most prosperous. It is our leading source of exports at this time. However, it is in great difficulty because the government of Canada has not made its position known. It has left a great deal of uncertainty about the safeguards in the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement. It is my firm belief, and indeed the belief of all those informed in the industry, that the government is about to give up the safeguards of the pact, but they have stated no policy. Not only are the workers concerned, but I know from personal conversations with leading managerial people in this country that they are concerned about what is going to be done with Canada's automotive industry.
The Liberal party has no policy now in terms of the automotive industry on this continent. If it has, it has certainly not revealed it. I have checked the record for the past year in terms of speeches made and questions asked in this House. I have found that the Tory party has no policy at all. It tries to come down on both sides of every issue, both with regard to automotive trade and everything else. They raise serious questions and then suggest that the government is not doing what should be done in the national interest. However, they make no concrete proposals whatsoever about what should take place in this very important industry, particularly in the province of Ontario. In the time remaining to me, I wish to deal with that industry and simultaneously with the important question of the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement. I will do this in terms of three myths that have been created. They have developed in part because of the deliberate failure of this government to shatter them.
The first myth is that the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement commits Canada and the United States to free trade. Over a period of years we are supposed to take down all the trade barriers and, so the story goes, have an open door to a free market. However, Senator Long, the CBC and the Toronto Star claim that Canada has reneged. They claim that we have not upheld our end of the promise and involved ourselves in the free trade program to which we were committed in 1965. This government has not come out and said that is a lot of hooey, which it is. The Canada-U.S. automotive agreement does not commit us to free trade. The government of Canada should make this clear. The people of Canada should know that is not the case. I will come back later to the importance of why it should not be a free trade agreement.
The other myth that has been allowed to develop in Canada, allowed by this government and not challenged by the media, is that the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement has been of fantastic benefit to Canada. The impression has been created that this is a colossally successful enterprise for Canada, and incidentally one having only
[Mr. Broadbent.l
marginal value for the United States, if indeed it is not a great handicap to the United States. Only two weeks ago, Premier Davis of Ontario said the auto pact had created 32,000 new jobs. That is a lot of hooey, as I shall show later.
The third myth is related to the other two. It is that after six years of automotive development in Canada, the renovation of our plants, the stimulation of new production techniques, we are now able to stand on our own feet without relying on safeguards in the pact. Has the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) denied this? Of course, he has not. Has the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) denied it? Of course, he has not. Has anyone in the government denied it? No. The fact is that we cannot commit ourselves to a policy of abandoning all these safeguards nor can we contemplate doing so in the future, and the government should say so.
I should like to give my reasons for suggesting these are myths, I should then like to propose some positive courses of action we ought to take and, indeed, must take if manufacturers are to be satisfied and if the people of Canada who work in the industry are to be satisfied. First, as to the so-called blessings for Canada. The pact came into being in 1965 because for many years we had been running a deficit on trade in automobiles and parts amounting to hundreds of millions annually. Something had to be done about this in Canada's interests, and so the pact came into being. One of the alternatives which was considered at that time, or one which should have been considered by the government, I do not know whether it was, was to rationalize our industry in the same way as the Swedes, the British, the Germans and the Japanese have done. We might have streamlined the industry, leaving only one or two firms, and possibly using an agency such as the Canada Development Corporation to ensure Canadian majority control. That would have been a viable alternative solution.
The other solution, the one recommended by Professor Bladen the one-man Royal Commission set up to consider this subject in 1960, advised streamlining on a continental basis with safeguards to protect both manufacturers and workers in Canada. This solution was accepted. It was accepted by the American manufacturers because it gave them a leading role to play in the industry in terms of future expansion in Canada. They were happy with it then, and they are happy with it now. There is no evidence to suggest that manufacturers on either side of the border are upset about the present situation. Indeed, most Americans outside the treasury department, including those who are members of legislative bodies, are happy about the pact.
What has been the effect of the pact upon Canada? Well, it has not provided 32,000 jobs since 1965, as Mr. Davis suggested, but only 13,000. Thirteen thousand jobs in six years is not a miraculous accomplishment. It is not exactly the second coming in economic terms. In that period, the market in Canada has grown. We might have expected a growth of employment in the industry anyway; it would have come about with the pact or without it.
Here are some figures with regard to employment and production in the industry. In 1965, we were responsible
December 9, 1971

for about 4 per cent of the total production in North America and consuming around 7.5 per cent of automotive products. We are still producing much less than we are consuming in Canada in terms of North American automobiles. At the present time we are producing about 5.5 per cent of the product and still consuming about 7.5 per cent. According to my calculations, if we got what was due to us in fairness and equity-and the Pact states in its preamble that there is to be fair and equitable production on both sides-instead of the 82,000 people who are now employed in the industry we would be entitled to employ approximately 114,800, an increase of 32,000.
I am saying that in terms of the employment of Canadian workers in this industry we are not yet employing the number of workers in Canada we would be entitled to employ if we were producing as much as we are consuming. My contention, therefore, is that instead of giving up the safeguards under the agreement we should be seeking to strengthen those safeguards. What is needed as a basic minimum is a commitment by the automobile producers of North America to produce in Canada, that is, employ workers, up to a level which would ensure we were producing at least the share of the North American market which we are consuming. This is the kind of policy the government should be pursuing. I would suggest to the Leader of the Opposition that instead of getting up every day to ask broad, general questions, coming down on both sides of every issue every time, he should put forward concrete proposals along the lines I have indicated if he is interested in the Canadian economy and in Canadian workers.
I am about to conclude my observations on the automotive industry. I apologize to the hon. members who know something of this issue for being so brief, but the time allotted to us is limited. There is another important question which must receive consideration by the government. It is: what is to be the future role of the supply of automotive parts in Canada. This section of the industry is presently of importance to more than 100 communities in Ontario alone; they depend for their livelihood on this sector of the industry. Right now, over 30,000 Canadians in 100 communities are not protected by the automotive agreement because automobile manufacturers are meeting Canadian added value requirements out of their own production and plant facilities. In addition to the 100 per cent CVA requirement for the industry as a whole, we need a further requirement which would make it mandatory for the assemblers of automobiles to meet their CVA requirement by getting at least 50 per cent of the CVA share from independent parts producers in Canada. I think it is essential to preserve the jobs we already have, and also to expand the number of jobs in the industry in order to meet in a rational and just way our increasing population needs.
I add that I am not simply making a protectionist argument in the traditional sense. We must have the one requirement or safeguard we need to protect the automotive industry in Canada in general since it is totally foreign owned and acquired. That is the gut purpose, if you like, of one of the original safeguards. We also need the related safeguard in order to ensure that we in Canada
Control of Canadian Economy
maintain facilities in this country to produce parts or components for automobiles. If this facility is not protected, and especially if the government, as I am sure it will, gives up the safeguards for two years, you can be sure, Mr. Speaker, that instead of people in Kitchener, Hespel-er, Galt, Oshawa, Oakville and countless other Ontario communities producing automobile parts, these jobs will go to the United States.
We need to protect the parts industry in Canada in the sense that we are almost an integrated market in terms of tariff policy in North America. We are not talking about protection in the old narrow, chauvinistic and technically irrational sense. My point is that we must protect the industry in the event that the automotive pact itself collapses in the next year or two. If the United States decides it is in its interests to repeal the pact, it can do so, as we know, by giving one year's notice. What is going to happen to the Canadian automotive industry if at that time we no longer have a parts industry in Canada? If that is the situation then no longer will we have an automotive industry of our own.
Therefore, I conclude with the following point. The leader of my party spoke very eloquently this afternoon about the need for more control of the Canadian economy and the development of manufacturing industries. He argued that this required an expanding use of public funds as well as a viable private sector. My final point is that the government has completely failed to make the private automobile sector viable on a continuing basis. The Conservative party has offered nothing at all in terms of constructive suggestions. It is the New Democratic Party alone which has a viable, creative and imaginative automobile policy for this country.

Control of Canadian Economy
As against this illusory, terrible ogre which has been brought up by the NDP and as against the gallant, dashing, knightly calls for a new strategy, what are the facts? It seems to me that the facts are very interesting. We may not have a new strategy but Canada and Australia are the only two countries of any major significance in the industrial world which lack a domestic market or its equivalent of at least 100 million people, and Canada, in spite of this drawback, has not done too badly. I am not sure how Australia has done. Last year we exported $16.9 billion worth of goods and we imported $13.9 billion. Relative to the United States, we achieved a surplus in trade of $3 billion. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Let us hear some facts.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
The problem is that Canada's total exports of goods and services amount to 25 per cent of our gross national product, whereas in the United States they are only 5.3 per cent. So, the Americans are not as concerned with our problems as we are with theirs. We may not have a policy, but 50 per cent of all the goods produced in Canada are exported and 40 per cent of these exports are finished goods, whereas 10 years ago only 12 per cent were finished goods. This is progress in the direction of the creation of jobs when we do our own finishing in Canada. It is illusory to say we have lost control of the situation and that jobs are being lost. We are frightened that if Mr. Nixon continues with his present policy it is certain that jobs in this country will be lost. But talking of the past, and of the record today, it is stupid and untrue to say that we have lost control of the situation because the situation is improving. The amount of manufactured goods we have exported has increased from 12 per cent to 40 per cent in 10 years.
We realize that the fact the United States is our largest market makes us vulnerable, but we continue to try through GATT to work for free trade and to expand in worldwide trade. We abhor tendencies toward the formation of trade blocs, abnormalities in currency values, U.S. economic measures against Canada and the world, but we abhor those against Canada and the world because we want a freer trade world; we want the United States to remain in that freer trade world with us and we want to remain in that freer trade world with the U.S. There is no way in which we who share this North American continent can separate from each other. Belligerent talk will not do it. Malevolent predictions that the United States are raising absolute Cain with us will not do it. We have to live together. In trade, Canada and the U.S. have exchanged last year the $19 billion worth of goods that I spoke about, which is 65 per cent of Canada's total exports. It is possible that that can be redirected to a certain extent, and we are trying to do that.
Certainly the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) had little or no success when 10 or 12 years ago he tried to do the same thing. Perhaps under the present climate and world conditions we will have more success. However, the fact remains that anybody who

December 9, 1971
Control of Canadian Economy
ignores the fact that 65 per cent of our exports go to the United States, and that we are terribly dependent on that market, is not facing reality. We know that 72 per cent of Canada's imports come from the United States. That should make us very important in the eyes of the United States. But this 72 per cent of our imports, of course, is only 20 per cent of United States exports. So, the United States does not feel as strongly about our trade relationship as we do. Nevertheless, United States sales to Canada are very significant.
I think the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have managed to get the message home. I believe President Nixon realizes, both from the point of view of trade and political stability, that he has to be sure his policies in no way hurt us unduly.
Each American bought $50 worth of Canada's goods last year. Every single American is a good customer. We each bought $500 worth of their goods. Every Canadian, to an American, is a very good customer. Thus, we are inseparable. There is no way we can be separated. This is the reality. Belligerent attitudes of undue nationalism will not solve problems because they are not part of this reality.
In reality we are together on this continent. There is no way for us to be anything else. Canada's external trade surplus was achieved in spite of the high value of the Canadian dollar last year and in spite of the serious increase in the volume of imports. This trade surplus is in the order of about $500 million in favour of Canada, which is another reason we have to think of the United States as being a good friend. In addition, the United States market is a finished and semi-finished market for our agricultural produce. This must become greatly expanded in the view of western Canada. We have to find new markets for our products and ways in which to finish new products so that workers can find jobs which are no longer available on the farms. We must find ways to bring these finished or semi-finished products to markets. What is better than the highly populated Pacific rim of the United States along the coast and what is wrong with carrying it on to Japan, China and Malaysia in that way? Without the springboard of the southwestern United States and its large markets, we could not begin to develop economies of scale in respect of the refinishing of agricultural products to allow us to compete in these other world markets. This is another reason, particularly in respect of western Canada, that we must treat the United States as our best friend and as our best trading customer.
Quebec and the Maritimes have similar problems with which I am not familiar, but I have heard from members of these areas that they are very concerned about the health and wealth of the United States because it is a good market for them. It is not all a one-way street.
The fact remains that we do need capital. Capital is mobile and capital can come from anywhere. If too much comes from the United States it causes anxiety and imbalances in our industrial structure. But surely it is up to us as Canadians, and especially as Canadian politicians, to decide what ground rules we want to make and what laws we want to operate under. That is not something to blame

the United States for and is not a reason to drive away investment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for the opportunity to participate in this important debate today. This is the second time within a few weeks that the general subject of the relations between the United States and Canada, and in particular the economic relations and the independence of our own country, has been raised as a matter of debate by opposition parties. I think this points up again, regardless of differences which may exist between hon. members, the rising importance there is in this question. It is certainly not a new question. Indeed, apart from the continual question of the relationship between English and French-speaking persons of this country, it is difficult to find a subject which goes further back into our history than the relations between those who live in the northern half of the North American continent and those who live in the southern half.
In 1971 a new sense of urgency arose. I think the initial guns were fired on August 15 when President Nixon announced a number of economic measures which were taken, not with specific direction toward Canada but because of the internal and external problems faced by the United States, of a nature which had a major impact on Canadians. Certainly, I for one have had to reflect again on the intimate relationship which exists between Canada and the United States. It is a cliche used so often it is like a smooth stone found on the beach to say no two nations have the kind of intimate relationship which exists between Canada and the United States. By the nature of that relationship, similar only I suppose to the marriage relationship, there are bound to be elements both of love and hate. In the last few months we have seen ample evidence of both. On Tuesday of this week, at the same moment the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made his report to the Commons on his recent talks with President Nixon, outside this building a group of people were protesting the sellout, if you like, or loss of Canadian sovereignty to the United States.
Canadians have lived for a long time with this ambivalent attitude. This may be one of the principal problems we have to deal with. When you live with a continuing problem like this day after day, year after year, and century after century, you tend to think the problem never really changes, that the factors are essentially the same and that how you feel and react to what our country or the United States does is really not of very much consequence because somehow the relationship will go on forever through good times and bad, as the marriage oath has it, in sickness and in health, for rich or for poor, and so on.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: I never heard of "and so on".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
"And so on" is a new revised version I have added. In respect of a marriage between Canada and the United States, it is important to reflect on the fact that a marriage can be dissolved not just by death, but by divorce or separation, and that there can be
December 9, 1971

difficult and almost intractable human problems. I think it is wrong for us to assume that all factors remain the same and that nothing changes. Life essentially is dynamic. It is not static. There are a number of factors that are quite new and which make it very important that we examine these questions specifically.
If we consider some of the events of the past few months, the sale of a major national press, Ryerson Press, which prints many of our text books, to an American interest, the loss of control of major oil companies, the earlier inroads made by American banking institutions into the Canadian scene, even more recently the controversy surrounding the leaked Gray report, the almost immediate visit of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to Washington and his comments on the discovery of a new understanding on the part of President Nixon about the nature and the authenticity of the Canadian nation, and only yesterday the release of a document on foreign ownership by the government of Ontario, it must be obvious that there is tremendous interest in this question.
Yet we are told by the Gallup poll released today that when people were asked what they thought would be the overriding issue in the next federal election, overwhelmingly they said it would be unemployment. American ownership was not even in second or third place. It was down in an almost imperceptible percentage position. Only a few people replying to the survey said they thought American ownership, American investment, would be a critical problem. Even the report released yesterday by the government of Ontario has warned us to think carefully about the promotion and exploitation of our natural resources, about allowing for greater foreign inroads into our natural resource sector to the discrimination of secondary manufacturing in Canada and said that this could create extensive unemployment.
I would say one of the problems with which political leaders, provincially and federally, have failed to grapple is the relationship that may well exist between either cyclical unemployment or increasing unemployment and inattention to the question of domestic priorities for the Canadian economy. If it is in fact true, Mr. Speaker, that we have inadvertently ignored some important questions in terms of the way in which we control investment activity in this country, and that this has discriminated against employment, we have misled the Canadian public on two counts.
We have to be circumspect about further American involvement in our resource industries. We must begin now-in fact, now is very late and possibly too late in some sectors-to define those areas wherein it is in the Canadian interest to discourage further American involvement and prohibit continued American monopoly. We have to define these areas and in some cases proceed to a process of rectification almost regardless of the cost.
These will not be popular words to certain segments of Canadian society but I feel they must be said if we are to protect the over-all standard of living that seems to be uppermost in the minds of many. I think it is fair to say that in our willingness and desire to achieve a standard of living equal to that of the United States we have often taken a shortsighted approach to the development of our 24725-25
Control of Canadian Economy
economy and particularly to tne development and utilization of our natural resources. This, again, is part of the Canadian ambivalence.
We cannot live so close to our neighbours and absorb as much of their culture as we do, from the moment we open our eyes in the morning until we close them in slumber at night, without experiencing a desire to achieve a standard of living equal to that of the Americans. And if the price of that standard of living is some loss of control over sectors of our economy, in the past we have not considered that cost to be too great. It appears that if we suffer loss of control over our natural resources we may also suffer a loss in our standard of living and so will have gained the worst of all possible worlds.
It seems to me that we must be extremely careful to examine where our present economic policies, our present taxation proposals and our present regulations, both federal and provincial, are leading us. It is obvious that we have not looked very carefully into this question. Indeed, one of the real problems for us in examining this question is the lack of trust that has existed in the federal government in exercising jurisdiction in these matters. If there is anything that the present government can be blamed for, it is its lack of trust in the Canadian people regarding this issue. The government has succeeded in the last few months in fogging-up or, if I may say so, "Graying-up" the key points that are involved in this area to the extent it is becoming increasingly difficult for Canadians to see the essentials of the issue in order that a reasonable and sane analysis might be made.
Even though cabinet ministers have resigned on much these same issues, to date the government has been unresponsive to these important questions. One of the fascinating things to indicate the dilemma presently facing us was the immediate reac ion of provincial Premiers following publication of the Gray report. It was fascinating to watch four Premiers from different parts of the country indicate the horror with which they viewed the suggestions in that report in terms of the adoption of a screening agency and such kinds of bureaucratic intervention that might take place on the part of the federal government. This said as much to me about the deteriorating situation with regard to confidence between the federal and provincial governments as it did about the nature of the problem itself.
It is understandable that the governments of the provinces become uneasy when federal initiatives appear to threaten their own efforts at bringing development to their jurisdictions. We can understand all too well the anxiety of the poorer provinces-I may say in passing that I represent one of those poorer provinces-that are faced with continuing uncertainty by foreign investors who through their investments might succeed in aiding the development and economic expansion of those provinces. That is an anxiety that must be dealt with by any group wishing to deal in a realistic sense with this problem.
In the first instance we will require an integrated approach that will have more to it than inflated rhetoric or nationalistic fervour. It requires more than leaked reports and unilateral policy positions. It requires, in the first instance, that there be the fullest possible consultation. Indeed, I think the word "consultation" for this government is too weak because in effect it means a telegram

December 9, 1971
Control of Canadian Economy
sent at some strange hour of the day. The government calls that consultation and then proceeds to do exactly what it had decided in the first instance.
That is not what we mean by consultation. Consultation must allow for a continuous interchange and exchange of views and the establishment of goals and priorities on which there is a consensus within the country. It is interesting that Premier Davis, in releasing the report on foreign ownership in Ontario yesterday, suggested that the government of Ontario would not move until there was some clear direction from the federal government.
Second, Mr. Speaker, there would have to be some form of agreement by the provinces-
