subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Because we are talking about a federal system, not a unitary system as is sometimes conceived by members of the government. If they are not prepared to recognize that we are in a federal system, this will have a very serious effect on the important question of economic self-determination. We must deal with the anxiety of the provinces, and that can only be dealt with in terms of ongoing federal-provincial development of national criteria on foreign investment and national economic goals.
I agree with my leader when he suggests that we must have an industrial strategy which takes into account the realistic economic situation of this country. We will not get that until there is consensus as to goals. Perhaps it points up the way in which the government has failed to grapple with this question when we consider what kind of priority it has given to the elaboration of goals in regard to regional disparity. Unless we take these issues seriously, none of the provinces should be asked to take this government seriously when it talks about a strategy for foreign investment and Canadian economic determination.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: It is not a unitary system. The provinces also have a responsibility to put forward a policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
I am glad that some members on the other side are beginning to see what is involved in a federal system. I hope the hon. member will say that in his caucus.
Another thing to be taken into account is the dramatic change in the direction of activity of the United States economy. It is too soon to predict with accuracy the course on which the United States is launched, but it is obvious that they have taken a firm hand in the direction in which they wish their economy to go. This will have a continuing impact upon us and will call upon us to make new decisions with regard to our economic situation.
I would remind hon. members that the decisions being taken by the United States are not only because of individual or short-term problems concerning abnormally high unemployment or rising inflation, but they are also related to the changing nature of the American economic

structure. This has changed very dramatically in the area of natural resources. It is only in the last decade or so that the United States has had to rapidly increase its importation of natural resources in order to meet consumer and industrial demands. We must pay attention to this matter because of our own situation, sitting as we do on the northern part of this continent with tremendous untapped natural resources.
It would be very easy for us in this decade to enter into attractive, short-term options which would make a variety of natural resources available to the Americans to satisfy their needs. However, we might discover in the latter part of the decade or early in the next that the requirements of the American economy would make it necessary for them to exercise the kind of choices and controls that would be completely unpalatable to the effective working of our economy short of a full economic and political union with the United States. In spite of the ambivalence that all Canadians feel with regard to the United States, I doubt whether there are many who would look forward with pleasure to an eventual and total absorption into that nation.
What is our task, then? Surely, our task for the moment is to consider in the widest possible way and with the greatest possible public discussion what our goals should be. We have talked about this in vague generalities in the past. I think the time has arrived when we should be specific.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext: Have you any ideas?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
I had the opportunity, and I hope we will have a further opportunity, to discuss this. I think in the short time that is available I can do little but set forth something to which I hope members on the opposite side will respond favourably. We must establish machinery for consultation that will work both ways. It must be identifiable machinery for the establishment of these goals which will involve provincial administration, which will involve key sectors of our economy such as industry, labour and the growing academic communities so there can be the fullest possible input in the discussion.
There must also be consultation beyond our borders. Sometimes I think we live in a kind of fool's world where we allow ourselves to be caught out because of lack of information of what is happening beyond our borders. Obviously, we must have machinery to receive information and for consultation in Washington and in the European countries where there is increasing economic activity.
There is also a need for comprehensive industrial planning. This includes an approach which will recognize that there are certain sectors of our economy that are crucial to our own development and the maintenance of economic independence. I think we have to begin the experiment and explore the possibility for diversifying our trade pattern which at the moment is extremely bilateral with the Americans, as well as diversifying the investment pattern and also enlarging it within this country. In many instances the main banking institutions in this country are more favourably disposed to large multinational American corporations than to Canadian business enterprise.
December 9, 1971

We must consider what steps can be taken to encourage Canadian participation in the investment in and development of industries in this country. Our industry is less efficient than it is capable of being, and does not use the industrial structures available. We must look to the development of our own technology and management expertise.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate on the subject of American control and foreign policy arises from the motion which reads:
This House calls on the government to institute without delay policies and programs designed to arrest further expansion of foreign control of Canada's economy and to regain control by the Canadian people of our natural resources and manufacturing and service industries in order to assure our country's independence and jobs for Canadian workers and to enable Canadians to shape their own national identity and social values.
This motion was moved by the leader of the New Democratic Party and is the subject of this debate. I shall deal with his speech later in my speech. First, I shall try to be constructive with the knowledge that I have, some of which was gained in the Canadian-American study conducted by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. We heard many witnesses from all walks of life who had investigated this problem. They were both Canadian and American. I believe that study was useful and the report has received the serious attention of this government.
What are the problems, Mr. Speaker? Any Canadian government seeking to formulate a policy on foreign investment faces the difficult problem of finding a balanced position. On the one hand it must consider the continued need in Canada of the new technology and highly skilled entrepreneurial technique which has traditionally accompanied United States investment in Canada. There is also the need to supplement the small Canadian domestic market with foreign markets, which accompanies United States investment in many cases, in order to permit economies of scale in Canadian production. Of concern is the integrated financial market between the two countries in which there is a large, twoway flow of capital and also the interdependence of the two countries in trade.
At the same time there are the following, additional complications to be kept in mind: (a) the provincial desire to promote regional development which leads the provinces to compete with each other in granting concessions to foreign investment bidders, and (b) the geographical and social proximity of Canada to the U.S. which makes unacceptable a markedly inferior standard of living for Canadians.
The government will be mindful of the advantages of U.S. investment, namely, the large capital inflows available for Canadian resource and industrial development, the advanced technology, the highly developed managerial skills, production techniques, financial and marketing skills which usually accompany U.S. investment, the resulting expansion of employment, the possibilities for
Control of Canadian Economy
increased exports due to access to expanded or new markets, the stimulus, at times only, to competition and the capacity of the multinational firms to develop economies of scale in production which may be impossible for Canada to develop indigenously in some cases.
There are also increasingly evident disadvantages connected with U.S. investment to be considered, particularly disadvantages related to the extraterritorial application, through Canadian subsidiaries, of U.S. laws and policies dealing with control of exports, anti-trust regulations and balance of payments, disadvantages associated with the leverage and manipulating power of huge multinational corporations and disadvantages related to the high concentration of U.S. ownership in key resource and manufacturing industries, with the attendant fears that important decisions made by such U.S. companies which have interests extending far beyond Canada may not be in Canada's best interests. These would include decisions regarding purchases, sales, research, processing, production, pricing and export sales.
With these considerations in mind, the government has open to it the following possible lines of policy and could use a mixture of both. First, there are restrictive policy possibilities. As in several countries, a government foreign investment agency could be established to regulate to a greater or lesser degree foreign investment. Second, there are positive policy possibilities. A bill to create the Canada Development Corporation was passed recently. The corporation is expected to be a leader in positive and imaginative government policies to increase Canadian control of the economy. It is intended to be a new and major source of equity capital for large-scale industrial and resource development, to help finance new Canadian-owned projects and to play a leadership role in organizing small, potentially uneconomic Canadian companies into larger, more viable enterprises through mergers or rationalization schemes. This is particularly likely to be applied in sectors of manufacturing where technology dictates economies of scale beyond the scope of the small firm or of the Canadian market.
It may enter into joint venture schemes. It will probably try to provide an attractive alternative to entice back to Canada extensive Canadian investment, both institutional and private, in the U.S. and will eventually offer its shares widely to the Canadian people. However, the corporation will not become a buy-back agency solely to protect Canadian companies from sales to foreign buyers. If those who keep knocking the Canadian Development Corporation will stop playing politics with it and give us their best ideas on the subject, the corporation will work.
The government could also introduce a whole range of incentives for companies to increase Canadian equity participation or Canadian personnel or to follow other of the government's guiding principles. As was suggested in the government white paper on taxation, capital gains on U.S. investment could be subjected to heavier taxation than capital gains or Canadian investments. Legislation could be enacted that would countervail the effect of the extraterritorial application of U.S. laws; for example, those relating to the U.S. anti-trust laws which may inhibit necessary rationalization schemes of Canadian industry. We must undertake research in technology and scientific development, expand our economy and make efforts to

introduce policies in other areas which would help to stimulate industrial development, strengthen competition and improve Canadian technological and managerial skills. These are policies which might tend to reduce the Canadian industrial dependence on foreigners. Measures could be adopted which would provide incentives for Canadian firms to expand their operations and investments abroad in order to capture new markets for Canadian exports. Also, the government could initiate talks with European countries which face similar problems regarding the extraterritorial application of U.S. laws and powers of the U.S.-based, multi national corporations with a view to possible concerted multilateral action.
Having said that, I believe that the government acted with courage and initiative in approaching the gigantic problems created by the United States. What did the government do? Immediately, as soon as it was aware of the difficulty, the government introduced the Employment Support Bill which in the short run will protect many jobs in Canadian industries. This was done without panic, with deliberately planned initiative. The step was taken promptly and was well thought-out. The measure appears to be working well, in this interim period, to alleviate some of the uncertainty that has been brought on by the American decision.

It was delivered by a frustrated member annoyed by the misguided wafflers in his party, the impractical visionaries and inexperienced professors, most of whom have never suffered the agonies of unemployment and who cannot themselves be dismissed from their secure university positions due to monopolistic rules governing the teaching profession. I resent the stagnation that comes from many parts of this House and I encourage all members to come forward as some have done in this debate with constructive, positive suggestions to make Canada a great, strong country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure whether I should check for dangling participles before or after I have spoken.
Control of Canadian Economy
There comes a point in any discussion of the necessity for Canada to maintain its political and economic independence when someone must pose the question: why do we wish to maintain political and economic independence? An attempt must be made to answer that question.
I think that the inarticulated major premise of any argument for Canadian political and economic independence is that there are some aspects of the Canadian culture which are unique and different. They are valuable and worthy of preservation, partly because of their unique quality. If that is not part of the thinking behind calls for economic and political independence there would seem to be precious little reason for pursuing those goals.
Human awareness of a situation is seldom, if ever, contemporaneous with the birth of that situation. There is a time lag between the creation of a new reality and a human perception of awareness of that reality. Thus, while Canadians were busily disentangling themselves from Britain whose power was on the wane another and very real danger to the continued existence, not to mention the flourishing of, a distinct Canadian identity, crept up on us. Donald Creighton, writing in MacLeans Magazine of November, 1971, describes the new threat in the following words:
The truth is that Canadians, in accepting American capital, American management and American technology, have unwittingly received the spirit that animates all three. They have not only become subjects of the American continental empire, but they have also become converts to its characteristic philosophy of life, to what might legitimately be called its religion. The central doctrine of this religion is a belief that progress is the only good in life and that progress means a liberation of man for the progressive conquest of nature by technology.
Professor Creighton went on to say:
This new doctrine (the doctrine of continual economic growth) has captured the minds of Canadians, just as it has those of every other people in the western world. To achieve economic growth, they are prepared to sacrifice their independence, pillage their natural resources, contaminate their environment and endure all the hideous evils of modern industrialization and urbanization. The American empire is taking over the birthright of Canadians; and its imperial religion has taken over their minds.
What is this new religion, as Professor Creighton calls it, replacing? What have we got to lose? Tolerance is one thing. Tolerance is a peculiarly Canadian virtue-a virtue and a vice, I suppose. Peter Newman made one of the best stabs at describing what is unique in Canada in the same edition of MacLeans in which is to be found Dr. Creighton's article. He said:
What we tend to say when we are exhorting our countrymen to stand up for Canada is that we need as a people to be more energetic in tackling our trade problems, to develop a stronger technology, to be less timid in our patriotism, more aggressive in pushing our own point of view-to be, in other words, more like the Americans.
But surely, what we have that is ours, the quality that makes us special as a nation, is almost antithetical to all of these admonitions. It's what Creighton himself calls our "inherited Canadian belief in an ordered peaceful society and a gentle and simple way of life! The Canadian character, by definition, displays a reticence, a disdain for xenophobia, a dislike of bombast, and a genuine desire to let each other be. In part, it comes out of being small, out of not having to be first, out of being able to encompass the indigenous in very different cultures of the regions without having to savage them in the name of some monolithic concept called Pan-Canadianism. There is something very special about a man from the outports, say, that may seem very strange to a man from

December 9, 1971
Control of Canadian Economy
the Peace River country. He is a Newfoundlander and he is a Canadian, but he can be both.
It is that which stands in danger of being lost. Realizing the fact that it stands in danger of being lost is perhaps the first step to preserving it.
To see that it stands in danger, we need only look around us. American-inspired fads and fashions, techniques of production and modes of consumption, standards of living, economic, social and religious ideologies and philosophies of life generally have become increasingly popular in Canada. It is probably safe to say that most Canadians eat much the same kinds of food, wear the same kinds of clothes and live in the same type of house or apartment as do Americans. Our respective educational systems teach much the same subjects, use similar techniques and attempt to inculcate much the same values. English-speaking Canadians and Americans read much the same books, magazines and comic strips, watch the same movies and television programs, respond to the same type of advertising and buy the same kinds and brands of automobiles, household appliances, clothes, packaged goods, cosmetics and patent medicines. They participate in the same types of sports and other recreational activities. They join branches of the same lodges, fraternal societies, service clubs, scientific, trade or professional associations. But in all of this similarity there is one hitch for those of us interested in preserving what is unique in this country: all of the similarities are American oriented, American initiated and American dominated.
This process has gone so far that many Canadians have come to think that making the effort to remain Canadian constitutes a sacrifice. They believe that instead of gaining something in strengthening our ability to be ourselves, we would be losing something. This is the most insidious thing about the situation in which we now find ourselves.
The manner in which our thinking is directed is both subtle and direct. Take as an example our social organizations. As I have said, historically Canadians have organized and joined branches of the same lodges, fraternal associations, service clubs, trade, scientific and professional associations as Americans. The presence of a large number of American social organizations, whether formal or informal, in Canada may well serve to reintroduce or reinforce American values which are already being presented to Canadians through the media of communications which are also American dominated. That may or may not be considered a threat to Canada. However, these social organizations, by acting as informal lobby groups for American interests or by determining the direction of social research, do conflict with Canadian cultural, social and political goals.
I mentioned a moment ago that the influence of the American media is exceptionally profound. Through the various communications media Canadians are made constantly aware of American social problems and America's reform tradition. Social issues which may or may not have originated in America are often popularized first by the United States. Due to the extent to which American technology, people, ideas and methods of operation are already present in the Canadian social structure, Canadians tend to absorb the popularized version-which is

American-of social issues in such a way that it tends to affect our ability to deal with similar social problems which become apparent in our own society. We accept the package deal. The reform element often adopts the style, the jargon and the literature of the American reform element. The rest of the Canadian population often acts on the judgments made about the similar American situation.
All of this process tends to ignore the fact that Canadian social institutions and Canadian social problems are often difficult clearly to define; in fact, the American influence makes their definition even more difficult. It also tends to ignore that Canadian social institutions tend to operate and respond in a different manner from American institutions and to respond to situations in a different fashion from their American counterparts.
Thus, through the American influence we may well be misdefining our social problems and misdirecting our efforts to correct them because both the statement of the problem and the structuring of the solutions are based upon experiences alien to our own in fact, but which seem to be our own because of the presence of the American thinking pattern in our media. We are perceiving our own country in a very confused manner and are not able adequately to deal with our problems because of this confused perspective.
Let us look at the situation in Canada with respect to our culture and the things that affect our culture. Of the 20 top television programs, only three are Canadian. Only 5 per cent of the book publishing industry is Canadian owned. Only about 20 per cent of text books found in Canadian schools are Canadian in origin. Forty-nine per cent of professors at Canadian universities are of foreign extraction. Only three out of 16 National Hockey League teams are located in Canada. Many of our outstanding artists and dramatists must leave this country to find employment and challenges that are commensurate with their abilities. Hume Cronyn, William Shatner, Lome Greene, Donald Sutherland, Norman Jewison, Rich Little, Paul Anka, Douglas Raine and a legion of others have left Canada in order to find a suitable outlet which did not exist here, for their talents.
This fact has produced some ridiculous situations which, if they were not so painful, would be laughable. For example, in today's Globe and Mail it is noted in Blaik Kirby's column that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has purchased from New York a new dramatic anthology for its next summer's programming. This program was made by Canadian stars with supporting players from Toronto. Some of the plays are written by Canadians. It was produced by CFTO in Toronto, yet our national broadcasting system had to purchase it from a United States company.
Having said that, I do not want to leave the impression that nothing has been done to preserve Canadian culture, because that is not correct. For example, the Massey commission gave rise to the Canada Council which has done excellent work in fostering the dramatic arts and the fine arts in Canada. A few years ago an attempt was made to assist Canadian periodical publications through changes in the Income Tax Act which quite deliberately discouraged Canadian advertisers from placing their ads in United States periodicals. However, the only thing
December 9, 1971

wrong with that was that two of the most popular United States periodicals in Canada, Time and Reader's Digest, were excluded from the provisions of the Income Tax Act, so that the purpose of the changes was defeated in the end. This part of the Income Tax Act must be changed and the exclusion of Time and Reader's Digest dropped. This will do more to encourage Canadian publications.
In the field of radio and television the CRTC has been taking bold and imaginative steps to increase Canadian content. It is a measure of how far down the road toward integration with the United States we have gone that most of the efforts have been met with screams of protest from special interest groups and the public alike. But if I may be permitted an aside at this point, not all of these protests lack justification. In its endeavour to ensure that the Canadian electronic media remain Canadian both in ownership and in content, the CRTC has not really looked beyond the nationality of the owners and actors who are employed. It has done very little to ensure that the distinctive character of Canada is reflected in our electronic media.
Thus, Winnipegers can perhaps quite justifiably scream about the potential dangers of suggested changes to the Income Tax Act for a local American television station because in all likelihood if the American television station is forced to close, and if the CRTC's anticipation that more money will be available for the production of Canadian television is realized, production facilities will probably be centred in eastern Canada. The actors will have to move to eastern Canada and once again the Atlantic provinces, British Columbia and the Prairies will be left out in the cold. Therefore, it would seem that in our attempts to solve the problem of cultural assimilation we must make sure that the solutions we propose will have the effect of accurately reflecting Canadian realities, the regional nature of this country, and we must ensure that the insensitivity of American capital to the nature of this country is not simply replaced by equally insensitive central Canadian capital.
A beginning has also been made in the film industry with the creation of the Canadian Film Corporation to ensure Canadian content in the area of popular culture. The Canadian Film Corporation has sponsored some films which have received deserved wide acclaim. It has also produced some real dogs. But I think the idea of the Canadian Film Corporation should be expanded and perhaps the corporation should start producing films specifically for showing on television since movies on television have a high audience appeal. The only major fault with the Canadian Film Corporation is that perhaps it is not adequately funded.
I think we are unduly sensitive about producing the odd bad film. Every nation in the world with a film industry produces more bad ones than good ones, and I do not know why Canadians should expect to be any different. That is not to say that criticism is not legitimate. It is. And the more criticism, the better the end product. But the critics should remember that experimentation is the essence of creativity and experiments have, by their very nature, a high failure rate.
Control of Canadian Economy
I would be very much remiss if I did not mention, in the context of the Canadian film industry, the contribution of the National film Board. I know that every member of the House is acquainted with the excellent work of that body and I need not go into detail. What is distressing to me is that when this government felt the need some three years ago to cut back on government expenditures, one of the first places to feel the axe was the National Film Board. This would seem to me to be a drastic mix up in priorities.
There is less reason for optimism in other facets of the Canadian culture. Our book publishing industry is 95 per cent foreign owned. In the last two years we have seen the sale of major Canadian publishing houses such as W.J. Gage Limited and Ryerson Press. We have seen the threat of the sale of McLelland and Stewart prevented, perhaps only temporarily, by the action of the Ontario government. We have seen the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) holding conferences with Canadian book publishers in order to hear their suggestions for improvements. We have heard statements from the minister that action must be taken, but no action has been taken.
We need to ensure that the decisions about what we are to read are made by Canadians with a Canadian point of view, attempting ,to meet Canadian needs, rather than by Americans. We must immediately embark upon a five-point program. First, we must establish a Canadian book development corporation which would operate similarly to the Canadian Film Corporation. It would provide loans for the publication of books in the expectation that any profits derived therefrom would be shared by the corporation. Moreover, those loans should not necessarily relate to a single book but, perhaps, to a group of books so that the losses sustained by some would be covered by the profits of others. This would be necessary in order to assure adequate diversity in the kind of books published.
Second, the federal government should provide longterm, low interest loans to Canadian book publishing houses through institutions such as the Industrial Development Bank. Third, funds should be made available by the Humanities Research Council and the Canada Council for the publication of scholarly and artistic works by Canadians. Fourth, a Canadian-owned book distribution system should be established in competition with those systems which already operate in Canada but which are American owned. Fifth, there should be efforts made by the government to get Canadian publishers to co-operate in the establishment of a Canadian book publishing house in the United States which would potentially increase the volume of sales of Canadian books. The need for such measures is well documented.
I have been informed, in answers to questions placed on the order paper, that in 1968, when W. J. Gage Company was still Canadian owned, 22 Canadian companies supplied textbooks to Canadian schools and provided only 40.3 per cent of the total textbooks employed by the schools. Since then, W. J. Gage and Ryerson have been sold to American interests, so the percentage of Canadian textbooks being supplied to Canadian schools by Canadian publishers is now probably down to about 20 per cent.
In the universities the situation is worse. A survey prepared by Mr. Rod McDermitt and Mr. Art Skolenski entitled "The Textbook Racket" points out that 80 per cent of all library and 92 per cent of all university bookstore

December 9, 1971
Control of Canadian Economy
purchases are books not published in Canada, that only 17 per cent of all post-secondary textbook sales are from domestic publishers and roughly half of this number are published on the basis of adapted rights, and that therefore less than 10 per cent of all university texts are of Canadian origin.
As schools and universities move into machine teaching the situation is likely to become even worse. Most of the material used in machine teaching is prepared in the United States. The results of this domination of our publishing industry by U.S. publishing firms is one of the major factors producing the kind of situation recently revealed in a survey conducted by York University in which it was disclosed that Canadian students identify more closely with American presidents than they do with Canadian prime ministers.
I have much more to say on this subject of culture. I wanted to deal with sports, for example, but I see I do not have the time. I would like to conclude with this final thought, that economic, political and cultural independence are closely linked and interrelated. If we are to have any one of the three we must also have the other two. That fact must never be forgotten by the government in its efforts to meet the situation. I hope with that thought in mind the government will get down to work and present us with the policies and the legislation we require to keep this country ours.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion we are debating today is a timely one, even though it was debated two weeks ago, because the problem of foreign ownership is so much in the public mind today. It was said that one of the prime reasons for which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went to the United States last Monday was to inform the President that there would be new restrictions placed on foreign investment in Canada, meaning in our case American investment in Canada. Indeed, the newspaper pundits have been suggesting that this is a carefully planned move on the part of the Prime Minister, because they point up the following event. On June 18 the government introduced a tax bill which incorporated major reforms in the field of tax advantages for Canadian businesses and tax disadvantages for United States-owned businesses operating in Canada. It contained other provisions to force Canadian pension funds and certain additional passive investors in this country to invest less in stocks listed on U.S. exchanges and more in Canadian equities. Then on June 29 the competition act was introduced in the House of Commons, containing major innovations in the field of regulating the activities of foreign firms entering the Canadian market through takeovers and similar devices.
Finally, on June 30, an act to establish the Canada Development Corporation was given royal assent but has not yet been proclaimed. The major, unstated purpose of the CDC is to give Canadian vendors of major profitable enterprises an alternative buyer. In the past it has been stated that only the United States has been able to acquire them. There is no doubt that the brunt of Canadian policy to curb foreign takeovers will fall most heavily on U.S. firms which have the greatest propensity to invest in Canada. There is no doubt that if there is a change in the Canadian receptivity to U.S. direct ownership capital, this

could precipitate retaliatory action by the United States. This would mean cutting off or limiting access to the United States bond markets or borrowing by Canadian provinces and municipalities.
Canada, as usual, in dealing with the United States does not want the United States to curb trade or to shut-out borrowing by our provincial governments in the American market. So it seems, from the answers given in the House by the Prime Minister, that he went to Washington to inform the Americans that he is about to make a significant announcement as to what Canada will do in the matter of foreign investment. Therefore, it seems likely that in the near future we can expect a significant announcement by the Prime Minister with regard to the value of keeping out foreign investment in particular areas.
The ill-fated Gray report which was leaked has been deliberately designed so that its main arm and its main weapon against foreign investment is the so-called screening agency. And we no doubt are to be shortly treated to an announcement by the government that such an agency will be set up. It seems doubtful that such an agency will be able to act in a fundamental way to safeguard our national interest. It will act only to safeguard the regional interests of Canada, and the area to be safeguarded in Canada by the screening agency is, of course, central Canada. That a better method of dealing with foreign investment must be devised, in view of what has been an ad hoc basis of this government's intervention, can readily be seen.
There is the former Dennison Mines case, where the government intervened at the last minute to prevent the sale of uranium resources. There is the Home Oil case, where at the last minute the intervention of the government prevented the sale of a Canadian company to a United States company on very doubtful grounds. Then, again, the government allowed the sale of a Canadian oil company to BP Supertest, presumably on the basis that this was an English company and not a United States company and therefore more desirable in respect of foreign capital.
In the recent action of the National Energy Board in barring the export of natural gas to the United States we have a further example of how our ad hoc system of dealing with foreign investment is being brought about. The price of natural gas has risen because of its pollution-free qualities. Since 1959, about $100 million has been expended by American gas companies in finding reserves in Alberta. The Alberta energy board had okayed the export of natural gas and felt the reserves would be adequate, but the National Energy Board, acting in some divine manner, reversed this decision and did not allow the export of natural gas. In appearing beforg the miscellaneous estimates committee, representatives of the National Energy Board revealed that their prime reason for doing so was that two plants in industry were experiencing difficulty operating in high pollution areas in Ontario, that it would probably be necessary to change to a less pollutant type fuel and that these hydro plants would have to be protected.
December 9, 1971

Even the National Energy Board admitted that the use of natural gas in hydro plants would almost certainly be short lived because coal is a much cheaper fuel and it is only a matter of the time and money, mostly time, necessary to allow the thermo generating plants to get in a position to use coal as a pollution-free fuel. So the decision of the National Energy Board was made not to export gas. This was a political decision made with a minimum of political effort.
These decisions of the government to move on an ad hoc basis were made easy from a political point of view. They discriminated against western Canada, which the present government feels it is entitled to do at any time. They discriminated in the field of natural resources, the nonrenewable resources which are such an emotional issue and which everyone has a vague fear some day will be used up. The general feeling is that we should conserve these resources for our own use. We perhaps forget that we sometimes use other people's resources, which we think is quite all right.
In any discussion as to limiting foreign capital in Canada we could well consider Mexican experiences. It was been widely suggested that Mexico has maintained political independence at low economic cost. Mexico's policy of expelling foreign equity investment from certain industries has been achieved largely by foreign borrowing, due to inadequate internal capital sources. Thus, dependence on foreign financing remains, although with greater emphasis on foreign debt financing. At the same time, the country's ability to service this debt has been undermined by inadequate export earnings, resulting partly from a declining world demand for Mexico's traditional raw materials and partly as a result of its protectionist policies which have not stimulated manufactured exports. As the balance of payments situation has deteriorated, Mexico has been forced into further foreign borrowing both equity and debt. In this sense, the Mexican strategy has backfired and the country as a result of its policies is being driven back into the arms of the foreign investor.
Mr. Speaker, the one way that Canadians can retain control of their economic affairs, unless they live in a regimented society, is by their own economic efforts. The government has been making the suggestion that we can limit foreign investment in a manner that is beneficial to us, with the assumption that all investment whether Canadian or foreign will go where the government directs for the public good. In effect, this is what the National Energy Board did in the recent refusal to allow the export of natural gas. Having first implied that gas exports would be available to foreign capital and allowing the investment to occur, the National Energy Board will not now allow the export of gas. Presumably this is for the public good. But whether this money would have been invested had it been known that gas would not be allowed to be exported is doubtful. Perhaps this is the reason one-third of the drilling rigs are now idle. If Canadians are to have economic independence and maintain the standard of living they fully expect, will publicly demand and will receive, unless we enter a police state this will require a high level of economic activity.
If we are to adopt a new economic strategy that will lead to some predetermined objective, we must face up to 24725-26
Control of Canadian Economy
the much more fundamental question of what type of economic structure we want in this country, and the choice seems to be between whether we want more and more of our goods and services to be produced by the government or whether we want a great amount of our economic activity to be in the private sector. It has been variously estimated that about 47 per cent of the gross national income is being taken up by the three levels of the government. This is still growing rapidly and will likely do so for some time.
Canada in the last 25 years has been fairly successful in achieving reasonably full employment, relatively stable prices, viability in the balance of payments and a more equitable distribution of income among regions. In this, although we followed inconsistent policies we were aided in the post-war period by the great movement toward freer and more international trade which accounts for about 25 per cent of the Canadian gross national product. Second, during much of this time Canada was able to maintain its exchange rate at below that which the market dictated. This stimulated economic activity. Third, during most of the time since the last war we have been able to import large amounts of capital to finance plant and equipment expansion and we have had a very special economic relationship with the United States.
Now all four of these basic factors that have worked so much in our favour have changed. There is no guarantee that international trade will expand, and there are signs that we may be entering a period of protectionism and trade restriction. We will not be able to maintain an artificial exchange rate for the dollar and, whether or not Canada takes any action, there will be much less inflow of capital to finance domestic expansion. We are entering a period of new economic relationship with the United States. It would seem very likely that what the Prime Minister considered his great breakthrough in Washington was really only a Mutt and Jeff statement. He received sympathetic understanding from the President but a rap on the skull from the President's officials.
Mr. Connally is not likely to be one who discriminates amongst his enemies, and Canada and its contribution to the United States deficit must reasonably be considered in this category. But, with this change in the international situation, will not Canadians still want a reasonably high standard of living, with relatively full employment and fairly stable prices?
I was most interested in the speech of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) in which he discussed the auto pact and its history. He pointed out that in 1965 the option open to the auto industry was integration as we have presently, with a wide variety of models, or one or two models with the Canadian auto industry going it alone. When we consider the latter course, with the Canadian auto industry going it alone, we must ask ourselves whether Canadians would be willing to accept the choice of only one or two auto models, and we should remember that the production of even a couple of models would have to be carried out under protection. I do not know if we can do this under present government policies that are consistently phasing out the private sector and replacing it with the government sector.

December 9, 1971
Control of Canadian Economy
In the process of passing Bill C-259 we witnessed a significant step in the direction of diminishing activity in the private sector. Today the Globe and Mail reported that there was 40 per cent less staking of mining claims in Ontario during the first nine months of 1971 as compared with 1970. In Alberta, one-third of the oil rigs are idle. There is almost certain to be diminishing activity in the private sector in the near future.
The emphasis in the new tax bill, decreasing by at least 50 per cent the value of the small business vis-a-vis tax, will not encourage the starting of new companies and their growth. The imposition of a capital gains tax, especially on long-term capital gains, is certainly not a good proposal at a time when Canada needs the best investment climate it can provide for its citizens. The taxing of international income of Canadian companies at a time when the Americans, under DISC, are reassessing their tax in this respect seems a particularly foolhardy move.
Canada is the only nation of a highly industrialized type-this was vividly pointed out in a recent survey by the Economic Council of Canada-that does not have tariff access to a market of at least 100 million people. The government keeps pointing out that Canada has the fastest growing labour force in the world and will continue in this situation for a decade. Surely, if Great Britain, with its 55 million highly industrialized population, felt it necessary to join the Common Market we must take a long, hgrd look at our trading relations with the United States. The present is not the time to be dampening private initiative with a restrictive competition act, with changes in the labour code that will prevent innovation and technological change, all of which must surely hamper industrial management in its attempt to meet competition.
Much has been said to the effect that we should have a highly developed manufacturing industry, but in fact only the Americans can afford to buy our high-priced manufactured products. All indications show that if we are unable to sell in the American market we will have to produce much more cheaply than we are now doing. The western grain farmer has learned this lesson to his sorrow. He is now selling grain in the markets of the world at a price below that which he got in the 1940s and with little indication of future improvement.
The best way for Canada to maintain its competitive position and its economic independence in the world is through the ability of its citizens to sustain the private sector in a healthy manner. Only this will allow the creation of the wealth that will benefit the community. The restrictive measures introduced by the government will only result in the production of less wealth for the country as a whole.
We must live on the North American continent, Mr. Speaker, and we must be a neighbour of the United States. We should be at least thankful that we are not a neighbour of the Soviet Union, something which the Poles and the Czechs have experienced to their sorrow. Just today a newspaper item reports a massive build-up of Soviet naval forces in the North Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Surely no one in Canada believes those forces are there for our protection. As a nation we may not have all
the things we want, but in our neighbour we have much for which to be thankful.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue of foreign investment in Canada is obviously an important one for Canadians generally and for the government. Therefore, I listened carefully to the remarks of the leader of the NDP and the leader of the Official Opposition earlier today. I was very curious to see if, after calling on the government to state its policy on foreign investment and criticizing it for failing to do so, they themselves had clear cut, definite policies of their own to put forward on this vital issue. I think it is clear, after listening to their speeches, that they do not seem to have such policies as yet. Although, Mr. Speaker, I will admit that the leader of the NDP at least made a sincere effort to appear to be saying something definite on this matter. But I submit that even he, in spite of his efforts, was in reality no less vague and contradictory than the Leader of the Official Opposition.
The leader of the NDP admitted, and I think this is quite a change from what he and his party have been saying over the past few weeks, that we must maintain close and friendly relations with the United States. I think these were his exact words. But then he complained when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) held what were very useful and important discussions with the President of the United States for that very purpose. The Leader of the NDP went on-this may be a switch also-to praise Canadian entrepreneurs, lauded the ability of Canadian tycoons and said we should have more of them. But then he said that they were selfish, that they were out for a fast buck and should be replaced by public irlvestment and public corporations. However, I noticed that one of the NDP speakers just a few moments ago was complaining that one of the public corporations he favours so much, the CBC, has just spent a lot of money buying American TV programs.
At one point the leader of the NDP called for policies to be developed and implemented with provincial co-operation, but a few moments later he complained that the federal government may want to see what provincial reaction may be to its policy proposals on foreign investment. I do not think he was able to answer completely the question of the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) when that hon. member asked whether he thought a provincial government should have a real say in a decision not to permit foreign investment to be made within its borders.

I was in the House, and if I could allude to something to which we are not supposed to allude until it is in printed form, we could check the accuracy of my remarks on this point. The Liberal government led by Prime Minister Pearson legislated with regard to banks, federally incorporated trust, loan and life insurance companies. It was also responsible for measures dealing with newspapers, magazines, radio and television broadcasting. The present government has continued these efforts, Mr. Speaker. It has acted to ensure a Canadian presence in the uranium industry and the oil producing industry.
The investment companies act contains a provision to help maintain a Canadian presence in the sales/finance industry. The revised Canada Corporations Act now provides for greater disclosure of the activities of federally incorporated firms above a certain minimum size, including foreign subsidiaries. This is the kind of action for which the leader of the NDP was calling.
Mr. Speaker, the tax bill before us contains incentives for Canadians to invest in Canada. There are the proposals on the investment of Canadian pension funds, proposals allowing the deductibility of interest on money borrowed for the purpose of acquiring a Canadian firm. There is the proposal for special tax concessions for Canadian-controlled small businesses, and the more general tax credit incentive to Canadians to invest in Canada rather than abroad.
The competition bill introduced by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) earlier this session contains provisions aimed at minimizing the
Control of Canadian Economy
extraterritorial impact of foreign legislation and decrees on Canadian business and trade and the Canadian competitive environment. It also includes a proposal which would ensure that international mergers should be reconciled with a reasonably competitive environment in Canada.
The Canada Development Corporation is now in operation, and in spite of critical comments from the other side of the House I am convinced that it will play an important and successful role in creating and strengthening profitable Canadian business activity.

speechtext:
I will send over another book and see if you can tear it. The Prime Minister has said that the government would be announcing its position on this matter when it publishes further background material. It is aiming to do so at an early date as it feels it is important that the statement of policy and this material should be presented at the same time to assist in developing a public understanding of its position and to assist the discussion that I am sure there will be on it across the country. While I am therefore not able to indicate this evening what the government's position will be, I think I can make some general comment about various aspects of the issues before us.
Firstly, Mr. Speaker, I think it can be said that domestically the total volume of savings generated within the Canadian economy has now reached a level which is by and large adequate to finance a fairly rapid rate of economic growth. In other words, in the aggregate we appear to have adequate savings in Canada, though this does not mean that sufficient capital is always available for particular needs and application. Secondly, internationally, recent years have seen a continued rapid growth of the multinational enterprise with all the challenges it poses for smaller business concerns and for national governments. These are merely illustrations of the kinds of factors which I believe must be taken into account in the development of policy.
There is also, Mr. Speaker, a growing feeling on the part of many Canadians that this high level of foreign control of economic activity poses problems for the performance of our economy and for our ability to decide on our economic priorities and our ability to implement them, as well as problems for the development of a distinctive Canadian culture and identity. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has suggested can be the case, foreign investors can create problems for Canadian industrial priorities. Let me make two points about what some consider to be the economic problems caused by foreign investment here. Firstly, these kinds of problems are likely to be only in part attributable to foreign investment. Such investment has in many cases come in to fill gaps
24725-26'

December 9, 1971
Control of Canadian Economy
that have existed on the economic scene-gaps in technology, management or capital market. Therefore, there is a role for general policies in the creation of an economic climate to encourage further efficient industrial activity, high levels of production and high standards of living.
Secondly, it would be incorrect to ignore the benefits that Canada has derived from foreign investment over the years in terms of economic growth, development of some of the outlying regions, access to relatively cheaper technology, access to foreign markets, and so on. These considerations suggest some of the elements that could form part of a foreign investment policy which would not involve Canadians paying an economic price in terms of their standard of living. In the first instance, I submit there is a place for measures to support and encourage Canadian entrepreneurship and Canadian abilities to undertake more of our own industrial development. I refer here to further measures to support innovation, technological development and greater efficiency in capital markets.
There is also a role for policies aimed at improving the general economic environment to help in the further development of sound industrial structure, with strong internationally competitive firms whether they are Canadian or foreign controlled. I think there is also a place for other measures pertaining to foreign investment. These measures must be flexibile, recognizing Canada's continuing need for foreign investment in some areas and the fact that both costs and benefits are involved and associated with it.
I should also like to point out to hon. members that a Canadian policy which seeks to ensure that foreign investment plays its part in the achievement of Canadian objectives would not isolate Canada in the international community. After all, other successful western industrialized countries have had comprehensive policies in this field for many years.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, the government has been working to develop a more comprehensive policy on the role of foreign investment in the Canadian economy. I look forward to this policy being announced shortly. I am confident that it will be consistent with the desire of Canadians to have at one and the same time continued economic growth and the ability to make fundamental decisions with regard to their destiny as a nation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even though we may differ sometimes with our good friends of the New Democratic Party because of our divergent views, I must say that I give my unqualified support to the motion submitted by the opposition as introduced by the hon. member of York South (Mr. Lewis).
It is obvious, in fact, that the present government is playing a double game. On the one hand, it hints to the Canadian people that it would welcome an independent economy mostly controlled by Canadians. On the other hand, it asks, begs or even insists that Americans invest in Canada.
I would like to attempt to show that these contradictory practices stem from the false principles on which our present economic system is based. Yes, in trying to render the financial system unshakable and immutable, we show contradiction and ridicule.
The motion before us is therefore very appropriate. We must come up with policies and programs designed to restrain increasing foreign control over the Canadian economy by foreigners, for it is urgent.
We are really and truly at the mercy of foreign control and to a large degree, at the mercy of the American giant.
On September 29 last, the hon. Minister of Industry and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) was explaining, during the symposium of contemporary Canada in Houston, Texas, Canada's economical dimension in the North American context. He said and I quote:
Every American bought for $50 of Canadian products in 1970 while during the same year every Canadian spent $500 on American products; this gives a per capita ratio of 10 to 1. If the Canadian economy is not prosperous, we are not able to buy all those products from your country.
Of course if we are not prosperous, we cannot buy for $500 of American products per head. But why do we have to buy? Why buy when those products are available in our country? Why buy when we can manufacture those products ourselves? In short, why base our own prosperity on that of the United States?
The whole speech of the minister, during that symposium, reflected the sickly timidity of the complex-riddled person, of the sheep that would all of a sudden like to be a lion. And I quote excerpts from the conclusion drawn by the minister on that occasion:
It seems the United States are moving in the direction of a policy of self-sufficiency and this country considers it would be more advantageous for it to import our raw materials and energy resources but at the same time to inhibit the development of our secondary industries we would be forced to reconsider very seriously the whole of our relations with the United States. In that case, we would have to reassess entirely our industrial and trade policies. It would no doubt be a "reassessment that would break our hearts"! However, I can assure you that we could not in any way drop the high priority that we have given and that we will continue to give to the manufacturing and processing sectors of our economy which are essential to an increase in employment in Canada.
It can be seen here how difficult it is to escape the erroneous basic principles of our economic system. We
December 9, 1971

are wearing blinders which prevent us from looking at other solutions that are so very simple.
When will we stop thinking of terms of foreign interests. When will we decide to change what needs to be changed, the economic system? We are so locked up in this foolish system that we forget elementary notions of mathematics and logics.
Mr. Speaker, it is true, as the motion indicates, that we lack policies and programs to give back to Canadians the control over their natural resources and their goods and service industries in order to ensure the independence of our country. Why? Because none of those who have been called upon to govern this country, the right hon. Prime Minister included, have had the courage and the strength to introduce the required changes. The recent Nixon-Trudeau meeting as points out Claude Lemelin in Le Devoir of this morning can open the door to a solution which we are all wishing for. I quote an excerpt from Claude Lemelin's column in Le Devoir of this morning:
One century of common life under the shade of the United States and their "manifest destiny", almost half a century of economic dependence on that ever growing power, the precariousness of their national identity, the frailty of their political unity have overburdened the Canadian people-whatever their language or their locality-with a serious inferiority complex coupled with deep intellectual alienation. How could they conquer that resulting collective feeling of helplessness which, for instance, threw the provincial premiers into a panic weeks ago when the Gray report leak dropped a hint of possible federal control over foreign investments?
No doubt, not very dignified was the decision made by the Prime Minister of Canada, in order to ever so slightly lighten that psychological mortgage, to go ask the American People: "Are you going to swallow us? Are you going to retaliate if we withdraw from your jaws?" However, taking into account once more the Canadian context, such canvassing could well have a liberating and disalienating effect on Canadian public opinion.
Mr. Speaker, this journalist is convinced the situation can be corrected. But I would emphasize that if we truly want to bring about changes we must first reinforce the weak foundation. If we want employment for Canadian labour, if we want to let Canadians themselves create their national identity and social values, we must endeavour to find the true answers to the following questions: Do we have the required natural resources? Do we have enough products? Can we produce or manufacture ourselves what we need? Do we have the required manpower?
Mr. Speaker, answering these questions is finding the solution.
Let Canadian industry have the exclusive opportunity, up to a certain point, of manufacturing all the products required by 23 million Canadians, let the farmers feed those same 23 million Canadians, in other words let us make here without foreign participation everything physically feasible by making it financially possible and this will be the beginning of a genuine solution to those problems we are all concerned about.

They are responsible for formulating policies. Did we hear about any tonight? We heard nothing at all. We heard the Minister of National Revenue say that the government had taken a number of steps in order to curtail foreign investment in this country. Immediately there came to mind the Reader's Digest situation mentioned by some hon. members to my left.
The minister also said that he cannot indicate what the government's position will be. That is what this motion is all about. It is criticizing the government for failure to come forth with some kind of industrial strategy for this country. He talked about economic growth. He told us that everything is rosy and everything is fine. He said this in the face of unemployment figures that are staggering, and in face of an announcement today that the cost of living index has risen by 4 per cent. He asked us to believe that everything is rosy. He gives these piddling examples as illustrations of how everything is going so well.
The minister talked about protection of our culture and our Canadian identity. One can almost use a southern accent and say, "With this government, we over on this side have nothing to fear about our culture and identity and we do not intend to be assimilated by those rascals down south." That is the size of it. There is a paranoid, almost pathological preoccupation with something they are trying to make political hay out of over there. They are trying to erect a great big bogeyman, as are the New Democratic Party members to my left. This great bogeyman of the United States is about to come here, clutch us to his bosom, suffocate all our Canadian identity and culture and squeeze us dry.
The minister also talked about Canadian entrepreneurship. I will tell him, as well as my friends to the left, what will bring about Canadian entrepreneurship. It is not more controls, suffocating tax measures, competition acts, investment incentive acts and new labour codes which insert government management into private man-

speechtext:
Consider the ten points the leader of the NDP trotted forth in his motion. He says there ought to be a government export trading agency. In other words, more control. It is like the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) when he introduced the minerals legislation for the Northwest Territories; he wanted to be able to determine when, whether and, if so, what volume of minerals could be exported. More state control, more state intervention.
Members to my left say they want standards of resource planning and development. Standards set by whom? By the government. More bureaucrats, more control. If they had their way everybody would be getting a government cheque, everybody would be employed by the government and told when to work and how much to work, when to go to bed, when to breathe and when to sleep. But that is not my idea of enterprise in this country. It is time we got back to good old, solid Canadianism, Canadian free enter-
Control of Canadian Economy
prise, Canadian initiative and Canadian incentive. We shall not get it if we listen to the half-baked philosophy which comes from my left, and we shall not get it from a government whose feet are directed solidly upon the road to socialism. We shall only get it if we increase opportunities for initiative in this country.
The mover of the motion wants to see an increase in public investment in the resource industries. What else is that except nationalization? I want someone over there to tell me if I am wrong. More public investment in the resource industries means only one thing-control of those industries by the state. The hon. member criticizes the tax concessions which have made the mining industry the second largest in the country. What is wrong with concessions which stimulate incentive and increase investment in the country? The hon. member favours planned shutdowns and the control of management decisions. He talks about myths. He says it is a myth that Canada needs foreign investment. He says businessmen do not believe they have the entrepreneurial skills which made this country what it is. I have not heard them say they lack these skills. Of course they have these skills, but they will lose them rapidly if the government pursues the road it is presently following and continues the kind of stifling and suffocating legislation which is halting the growth of the country.
He says there must be co-operation with the provinces. You bet your tiddly there must be co-operation with the provinces.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FOREIGN OWNERSHIP TO REGAIN CONTROL OF THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are about three minutes left before the division bells are due to ring and I want to see whether in that time I can get the House to face the real problem.
I have heard it said that this whole problem is connected with America, that it is an American problem. I have heard it said that the Americans are lovely people. It doesn't really affect the issue much. The fact is that our ills arise from corporate control. This mechanism, which was devised to allow people to build an enterprise, has grown so big and powerful as to become almost a Frankenstein. The government and this nation has a purpose in mind, which is of course the interests of the people of Canada. Similarly, the United States has its purpose in mind. But the only purpose a corporation can have in mind is to make money. Profit must be, and always has been, the main and only purpose of corporate structures.
What our real problem is is not anti-Americanism or Canadian control of our own economy. The United States is having the same trouble with its corporate structures as we are. United States multinational corporations have invested in Europe and elsewhere, taken advantage of production facilities in Taiwan and other countries, and have brought goods back to the United States. This cannot be the fault of the people of the United States or

December 9, 1971
Control of Canadian Economy
the government of the United States. If hon. gentlemen opposite regard IBM, Minneapolis Honeywell, and other large corporations as an adjunct of the United States government, surely they must say that Seagrams is an adjunct of our government, and I do not think they can say that.
So we must face what is the real issue here. To bypass the issue by saying that it does not exist, as did the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), is not the way to tackle the problem. The problem is vast, and it is vast because it has created in Canada the situation where the growth, its distribution and direction, of our life style is no longer within the control of our elected representatives but is really under the control of corporate structures that have served their purpose. Let us not deny that there was a reason for this. There is always a good reason for a corporate structure. But to say that free enterprise must go on in perpetuity is no answer to the problem.
I see my time is just about finished, so I am unable to deal with the other aspects I wanted to mention. But let me say this. If I have gotten across to the members of this House that we should not be anti-American, then I have done a lot. It is easy for a politician to be anti-something. I agree with the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) that it is easy to say that Americans are our enemies, but this will not do the nation any good.
